sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Authentication spans both layers of a fullstack application. Interviewers ask whether you can explain the end-to-end flow, not just paste a code snippet. Knowing why JWT is stateless, where to store it safely, and how Spring Security validates it will set you apart from freshers who only know the 'happy path' login.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
- **Session-based auth**: server stores session in memory/DB, client sends JSESSIONID cookie on every request.
- **JWT auth**: server issues a signed token, client stores it and sends it on every request — server needs no session state.
- **localStorage** is vulnerable to XSS; **HttpOnly cookie** is safe from XSS but needs CSRF protection.
- **Access token** (short-lived, 15 min) + **refresh token** (long-lived, 7 days) = standard production pattern.
- **Spring Security JWT filter**: intercept every request, extract token from Authorization header, validate signature, set SecurityContext.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- JWT structure: header.payload.signature — know what each part contains.
- Login flow: POST /auth/login → validate credentials → issue JWT → client stores it.
- Protected route in React: check auth state, redirect to /login if not authenticated.
- Spring Security: OncePerRequestFilter extracts JWT, validates it, populates SecurityContextHolder.
- XSS steals tokens from localStorage; CSRF forges requests using cookies — these are different attack vectors.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- "Where do you store a JWT token and why?" → HttpOnly cookie is safest; localStorage is convenient but XSS-vulnerable.
- "What is the difference between authentication and authorisation?" → Authentication = who are you; authorisation = what are you allowed to do.
- "How does the server validate a JWT without storing it?" → Verifies the signature using the secret key; checks expiry claim.
- "What happens when a JWT expires?" → Client uses refresh token to get a new access token silently.
- "How do you protect a React route so only logged-in users can access it?" → ProtectedRoute component checks auth state and redirects to login.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"In my project, I implemented JWT authentication. The user POSTs their credentials to /auth/login, Spring Boot validates them, creates a JWT signed with a secret key, and returns it. The React frontend stores the token in an HttpOnly cookie to protect against XSS. Every subsequent request includes the token, and a Spring Security filter validates the signature and expiry before allowing access. When the access token expires, the frontend uses the refresh token to get a new one silently."*
